full_text_en:
Chen Chao v. Jinan Urban Public Passenger Transport Management Service Center — dispute over administrative penalty for passenger transport management

Ruling Summary

With the integrated development of “Internet+” and traditional industries, the phenomenon of “ride-hailing” has emerged in the passenger transport market. This form indeed has actual demand among many cities and certain groups of people and has objectively existed. However, like traditional taxi passenger transport operations, this type of passenger transport behavior also concerns the safety of citizens’ lives and property, as well as the government’s orderly management of the public service sector, and shall be conducted lawfully and orderly within the framework of laws and regulations. For lawsuits arising from such issues, courts shall adhere to the principle of taking facts as the basis and the law as the criterion, and make comprehensive consideration and judgment by combining issues such as the social harmfulness of the conduct involved, the propriety of the administrative penalty procedure, and the principle of proportionality in administrative penalties.

Plaintiff: Chen Chao, male, 30 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Qufu City, Shandong Province.

Defendant: Jinan Urban Public Passenger Transport Management Service Center, domiciled at: Shizhong District, Jinan City.
Legal Representative: Cui Bing, Director of the Center.

Plaintiff Chen Chao filed a lawsuit with the People’s Court of Shizhong District, Jinan City, Shandong Province, due to a dispute over an administrative penalty with the defendant Jinan Urban Public Passenger Transport Management Service Center (hereinafter referred to as Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center).

Plaintiff Chen Chao alleged: The defendant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center issued the “Administrative Penalty Decision” (Lu Jijiao (01) Fa (2015) No. 8716) on February 13, 2015, finding that Chen Chao illegally engaged in passenger taxi transport operations, violating the provisions of Article 69, Paragraph 2 of the “Shandong Province Road Transport Regulations,” and decided to order cessation of the illegal act, impose a fine of RMB 20,000, and confiscate illegal gains. This administrative penalty decision had numerous issues, such as incorrect penalty subject, erroneous factual findings, illegal enforcement procedures, and incorrect application of law, seriously infringing upon his legitimate rights and interests. He requested that the court revoke the “Administrative Penalty Decision” (Lu Jijiao (01) Fa (2015) No. 8716) issued by Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center on February 13, 2015, in accordance with the law.

Defendant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center argued: 1. As the administrative authority for passenger taxi transport in Jinan City, it had the right to impose penalties on acts of engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission. 2. Plaintiff Chen Chao provided “online car-hailing passenger transport services,” and his vehicle did not have a valid operating permit, which constituted engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission. The above facts were corroborated by evidence including Chen Chao’s own admission in a subsequent media interview, on-site video recordings, on-site records, and investigation records, so the factual findings of the appealed penalty decision were clear. 3. During the enforcement processes such as investigation, notification, and service, law enforcement officers presented their law enforcement credentials and heard Chen Chao’s statements and defenses, so the procedures of the appealed penalty decision were lawful. 4. Chen Chao’s above-mentioned business conduct violated Article 8 of the “Shandong Province Road Transport Regulations” and Article 16 of the “Jinan City Urban Passenger Taxi Transport Management Regulations.” The defendant made the appealed penalty decision in accordance with Article 69, Paragraph 2 of the “Shandong Province Road Transport Regulations” and Article 41 of the “Jinan City Passenger Taxi Transport Management Regulations,” with correct application of law. In summary, the appealed penalty decision was lawful, and it requested that Chen Chao’s claims be dismissed.

The People’s Court of Shizhong District, Jinan City, Shandong Province, found the following facts at first instance:

On January 7, 2015, two passengers contacted Plaintiff Chen Chao via a ride-hailing software application, agreeing that Chen Chao would drive the passengers from near the August 1st Overpass in Jinan City to Jinan West Railway Station, with the passengers paying the fare. At approximately 11:00 a.m. that day, when Chen Chao drove his private car (license plate number Lu AVXXXX) to the drop-off platform at Jinan West Railway Station, staff of the defendant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center conducted an investigation, finding that Chen Chao had not obtained a taxi passenger transport qualification certificate and the vehicle he drove had not obtained a vehicle operating permit. The Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center considered that Chen Chao was suspected of engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission, issued an “Administrative Compulsory Measure Decision” to him, and seized his vehicle. On January 26, 2015, the Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center served on Chen Chao the “Notice of Illegal Act” (Lu Jijiao (01) Wei Tong (2015) No. 8716), stating that he was suspected of engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission, and intended to impose a fine of RMB 20,000 and confiscate illegal gains. Chen Chao subsequently requested a hearing. During the hearing, the case-handling personnel of the Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center presented Chen Chao’s illegal facts, relevant evidence, and proposed handling opinions, while Chen Chao challenged the fact-finding, application of law, and enforcement procedures. On February 13, 2015, the Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center issued the “Administrative Penalty Decision” (Lu Jijiao (01) Fa (2015) No. 8716) and served it on Chen Chao, citing that his illegal operation of passenger taxi transport violated Article 69, Paragraph 2 of the “Shandong Province Road Transport Regulations,” ordering cessation of the illegal act, imposing a fine of RMB 20,000, and confiscating illegal gains. Chen Chao disagreed and filed an administrative lawsuit within the statutory period.

It was further found: According to the “Notice on Printing and Distributing the Interim Provisions on the Main Responsibilities, Internal Organization, and Staffing of the Jinan Municipal Public Utility Bureau” (Ji Zheng Ban Fa (2004) No. 42) issued by the General Office of Jinan Municipal People’s Government, the defendant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center was a self-funded public institution responsible for operational guidance and technical services for the urban public passenger transport industry, assisting relevant departments in formulating service standards for public transport and passenger taxis, and undertaking supervision and inspection duties. According to the “Provisions on the Main Responsibilities, Internal Organization, and Staffing of the Jinan Municipal Transportation Bureau” (Ji Zheng Ban Fa (2010) No. 22), when Jinan’s institutional functions were adjusted in 2010, the Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center was transferred as a whole unit from the Jinan Municipal Public Utility Bureau to the Jinan Municipal Transportation Bureau along with the adjustment of administrative functions. It was now a public institution with independent legal personality under the Jinan Municipal Transportation Bureau.

The People’s Court of Shizhong District, Jinan City, held at first instance:

In recent years, with the integrated development of “Internet+” and traditional industries, acts of providing passenger transport services through ride-hailing software have emerged in the market. This case involved an administrative penalty imposed on ride-hailing transport operations, and the issues in dispute focused on the following two aspects:

1. Whether Plaintiff Chen Chao’s conduct constituted engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission

In this case, after contacting passengers through ride-hailing software, Plaintiff Chen Chao used a vehicle without an operating permit to transport the passengers from near the August 1st Overpass in Jinan City to Jinan West Railway Station, and collected a fare as agreed. Whether the above conduct fell within the scope of “engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission” as defined in Article 8 of the “Shandong Province Road Transport Regulations” and Article 16 of the “Jinan City Urban Passenger Taxi Transport Management Regulations” gave rise to two different views: One view held that such conduct was illegal, and the legal provisions were clear and unambiguous. Chen Chao’s vehicle did not have an operating permit, and he collected a fee from the passengers, which fully satisfied all the statutory factual elements of “engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission” under Article 8 of the “Shandong Province Road Transport Regulations” and Article 16 of the “Jinan City Urban Passenger Taxi Transport Management Regulations.” Another view held that the entry of ride-hailing into the taxi market was inevitable and consistent with the laws of social development, and therefore, the above provisions should not be used to negate the business model of the new format.

Ride-hailing, as a new format of passenger transport service, as a product of the sharing economy, its operation helps to improve the utilization efficiency of idle resources, alleviate the conflict between supply and demand in terms of time and space for transport services, and help to meet the actual needs of the people to a greater extent. Therefore, when a new technology or new business model emerges, based on considerations of competition philosophy and public policy, it cannot be simply excluded from the market, otherwise economic development would gradually slow down and eventually stagnate. However, it is equally undeniable that the operation of ride-hailing requires effective supervision. Like traditional taxi passenger transport operations, the passenger transport behavior of ride-hailing also concerns the safety of the public’s life and property and the government’s orderly management of the public service sector, and shall be conducted lawfully and orderly within the framework of laws and regulations. As long as laws and regulations are effective, they should be generally respected and enforced; this is a basic requirement of the spirit of the rule of law and an important manifestation of a society governed by the rule of law. Therefore, in this case, we must examine the legality of the appealed administrative act based on existing effective laws and regulations to reflect the authority and seriousness of the law, while also fully considering relevant factors such as social demands stimulated by technological progress and market innovation, making a judicial judgment that meets the current requirements of law-based administration while leaving appropriate room for future social development and legal changes.

In summary, Plaintiff Chen Chao’s conduct constituted engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission, violating the provisions of current laws. However, considering the special background of the new format of the sharing economy, namely ride-hailing, the social harmfulness of this conduct was relatively minor. Therefore, in the trial of this case, special attention should be paid to whether the administrative penalty was excessively heavy.

2. Whether the penalty range of the appealed administrative penalty decision was excessively heavy

Administrative penalties shall adhere to the principle of proportionality, ensuring that the penalty matches the offense. The penalty result shall be commensurate with the facts, nature, circumstances, and degree of social harm of the illegal act, so as to achieve the purpose of preventing the recurrence of the illegal act. In this case, Plaintiff Chen Chao used ride-hailing software to engage in road transport operations. The defendant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center did not provide evidence to prove the relationship between the plaintiff and the ride-hailing platform, nor whether the fares ultimately generated with the passengers were actually paid or settled, nor which parties benefited, leaving these matters unclear. Therefore, although the defendant could impose penalties in accordance with the law for engaging in taxi passenger transport operations without permission, in the conduct of road transport operations involved in this case, the plaintiff only actually carried out part of the conduct. Under the existing evidence, the defendant attributed all the illegal acts and their consequences targeted by this administrative penalty to the plaintiff and imposed a relatively heavy administrative penalty on him individually, resulting in an excessively heavy penalty range and amount, which constituted obvious impropriety. In accordance with the spirit of Article 70 of the “Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC,” such a penalty should be revoked according to law. Furthermore, the content of an administrative penalty decision shall be clear and specific, stating the facts and evidence of the administrative counterpart’s violation of laws, regulations, or rules. In this case, the administrative penalty decision made by the defendant did not specify the time, place, process, and specific circumstances of the plaintiff’s illegal facts and related road transport operations. On this ground as well, it should be revoked. As for the plaintiff’s arguments regarding the wrong penalty subject and illegal enforcement procedures, upon review, the defendant’s corresponding defenses were established, and the plaintiff’s above claims were not supported. In conclusion, the People’s Court of Shizhong District, Jinan City, in accordance with Article 70, Item (6) of the “Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC,” rendered the following judgment:

Revoke the “Administrative Penalty Decision” (Lu Jijiao (01) Fa (2015) No. 8716) made by the defendant Jinan Urban Public Passenger Transport Management Service Center on February 13, 2015. Court acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by the defendant Jinan Urban Public Passenger Transport Management Service Center.

The Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center was dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment and filed an appeal to the Jinan Intermediate People’s Court of Shandong Province, stating: 1. The first-instance judgment held that the appealed administrative penalty decision constituted obvious impropriety and should be revoked, which was unfounded. The social harmfulness of the appellee Chen Chao’s illegal operation was not “minor” as found by the first-instance court, and the first-instance court had not investigated this issue. The appellant’s imposition of a fine of RMB 20,000 was in compliance with legal provisions and did not constitute excessive severity. Evidence of settlement between Chen Chao and the passengers was not necessary evidence for investigating illegal operations, and the relationship between Chen Chao and the “ride-hailing platform” did not affect the penalty range for Chen Chao. At the time the appellant made the appealed penalty decision, the “ride-hailing platform” company had not been brought under administrative supervision, and the appellant had no enforcement or penalty authority over it. 2. The content stated in the administrative penalty decision complied with legal provisions. The “Administrative Penalty Law of the PRC” does not require an administrative penalty decision to specify the time, place, process, and other specific circumstances of the illegal facts. The appellant had already informed Chen Chao of the nature and circumstances of his conduct, as well as the reasons and basis for the proposed penalty, in other legal documents, without infringing upon any of Chen Chao’s rights. In summary, the first-instance court exceeded the facts of the case and rendered a judgment based on the special background that ride-hailing is a new format, which was clearly improper. It requested that the first-instance judgment be revoked according to law and that Chen Chao’s claims be dismissed.

Appellee Chen Chao did not submit a written defense.

None of the parties submitted new evidence to the court during the second instance.

The Jinan Intermediate People’s Court of Shandong Province, after the second instance, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

The Jinan Intermediate People’s Court of Shandong Province held at second instance:

1. Whether the appealed administrative penalty decision constituted obvious impropriety

The principle of proportionality is an important principle of administrative law, and administrative penalties shall adhere to the principle of proportionality. The imposition of an administrative penalty on a party must be commensurate with the facts, nature, circumstances, and degree of social harm of the illegal act. As a new format of passenger transport service and a product of the sharing economy, ride-hailing helps alleviate the conflict between supply and demand in passenger transport services, meet the public’s diversified travel needs, and aligns with social development trends and innovation demands. It should be treated with appropriate tolerance. On the other hand, this new format also brings negative impacts on the existing passenger transport management order and even poses safety risks, so it indeed requires strengthened regulation and guidance. The issuance of the “Interim Measures for the Administration of Online Car-Hailing Services” also corroborates this from a side perspective. When a new thing plays a positive role in meeting social needs and promoting innovation and entrepreneurship, the assessment of the social harm it brings should not only comply with existing laws and regulations but also fully consider whether it aligns with general public perception. In this case, the appellee Chen Chao’s conduct of using ride-hailing software for road transport operations had relatively minor social harmfulness, which was consistent with general social cognition. When administrative authorities impose penalties on such conduct in accordance with existing laws and regulations, they should minimize and limit the adverse impact on the party to the smallest possible extent, so as to achieve a balance between achieving administrative objectives and protecting new things. Furthermore, there were multiple parties benefiting from this conduct, and whether the ultimately generated fares had been actually paid or settled was not proven by the appellant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center with evidence. Given that the above facts remained unclear and the social harmfulness of the conduct was relatively minor, attributing all consequences of the conduct to the appellee and imposing a relatively heavy penalty on him individually violated the principle of proportionality and constituted obvious impropriety. The first-instance court found that the penalty range and amount were excessively heavy and revoked the appealed administrative penalty decision, which complied with the law. The appellant’s objections that there was no excessive severity, that settlement evidence did not affect the penalty range, and that the appellee’s conduct had minor social harmfulness were all untenable.

2. Whether the content stated in the administrative penalty decision in this case complied with legal provisions

Article 39, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the “Administrative Penalty Law of the PRC” provides that an administrative penalty decision shall state the facts and evidence of the violation of laws, regulations, or rules. Although the above legal provision does not clearly specify the extent to which the “facts” recorded must meet, the administrative penalty decision, as a written proof of the penalty imposed by the administrative authority on the party, shall record specific and definite facts, including the time, place, process, and circumstances of the determined illegal facts, so that the party clearly understands the factual basis for the penalty, thereby achieving the purpose of warning against the recurrence of the illegal act. In this case, the illegal fact recorded in the administrative penalty decision concerning the appellee Chen Chao was “illegal operation of passenger taxi transport,” but it did not specify the appellee’s specific illegal facts, i.e., the time, place, process, and specific circumstances of the illegal facts and related transport operations. The recorded items did not meet the requirement of being specific and definite. The first-instance court found that the content stated in the administrative penalty decision made by the appellant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center did not comply with legal provisions and should be revoked, which was proper. Furthermore, the facts recorded in the administrative penalty decision are the illegal facts ultimately determined by the administrative authority. The recording of specific illegal facts in other legal documents cannot replace the recording of facts in the administrative penalty decision. The appellant’s arguments that it had recorded specific illegal facts in other legal documents and had not infringed upon the appellee’s legitimate rights and interests were untenable.

In summary, the first-instance judgment had clear factual findings, correct application of laws and regulations, and lawful procedures, and should be upheld according to law. The appellant Jinan Passenger Transport Management Center’s grounds of appeal were untenable, and its appeal request was not supported.

Accordingly, the Jinan Intermediate People’s Court of Shandong Province, in accordance with Article 89, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the “Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC,” rendered the following judgment:

Appeal dismissed and the original judgment affirmed. Court acceptance fee of RMB 50 for the second instance shall be borne by the appellant Jinan Urban Public Passenger Transport Management Service Center.

This judgment is final.
